This page corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 53-7041.00 occupation "Hoist and Winch Operators" (hoist and winch operators): operating or tending hoists or winches to lift and pull loads using power-operated cable equipment. Official scope text: Operate or tend hoists or winches to lift and pull loads using power-operated cable equipment. The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 data and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET; the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; the two jurisdictions and their safety systems must not be applied to one another.

To judge whether hoist and winch operating suits you, first run one verifiable task drill using public or simulated materials: choose a clear lifting scenario (for example, using a winch to pull a length of pipe in a confined site), and write a step-by-step work plan from receiving the task, verifying the load and rigging, and checking the equipment and brakes, to confirming signals and personnel positions, then lifting, positioning, unloading, and wrapping up, marking the safety check points and possible abnormalities at each step (load over limit, worn rigging, brake failure, unclear signals, personnel entering the danger zone). Afterward, check: whether load and rigging verification, signal confirmation, and personnel isolation are treated as non-omittable items; whether abnormalities are written as stop-and-escalate; and whether you have marked which matters exceed your individual operating authorization (approving lifting plans, load testing, equipment modification). Test with a real deliverable, not just answers to an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | The work activity importance ratings for U.S. O*NET 53-7041.00 show that repairing and maintaining mechanical equipment (81), handling and moving objects (79), controlling machines and processes (78), getting information (78), operating vehicles, mechanized devices, or equipment (78), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (77), and monitoring processes, materials, or surroundings (77) are the most important activities for this occupation; work context shows that wearing common protective or safety equipment 91% report every day, exposure to high places 70% report every day, exposure to hazardous conditions 50% report every day, exposure to very hot or very cold temperatures 45% report every day, responsibility for others' health and safety 59% report very high responsibility and 41% report high responsibility, consequence of error 36% report extremely serious and 53% report serious, importance of being exact or accurate 84% report very important, and work schedule 72% report irregular (varying with weather, production, or contract deadlines). The most important skills are critical thinking (69), monitoring (66), and active listening (60). If you are willing to do repetitive mechanical work to procedure outdoors, in confined spaces, or at height, and to take direct responsibility for load and personnel safety, these daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (53-7041.00): responsibility for others' health and safety 59% report very high responsibility, consequence of error 36% report extremely serious and 53% report serious, exposure to hazardous conditions 50% report every day, exposure to high places 70% report every day, wearing specialized protective equipment 34% report every day, and work schedule 72% report irregular. This occupation deals with loads, cables, rigging, and site personnel: a single misjudged load, a single missed brake or rigging check, or a single misread signal can cause casualties and major property loss. This page therefore lists load and rigging verification, safety isolation, stopping and escalating on abnormalities, and authorization boundaries separately. On the U.S. side, this occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook, and the O*NET summary shows a projected decline (-1% or lower) from 2024 to 2034, with about 300 job openings per year, and a small employment size (about 2,700 in 2024). If it is hard for you to sustain outdoor and at-height work, irregular shifts, and direct safety responsibility over the long term, you should treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Commitment judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things on the same job at once: make the operation solid (complete load verification, signal confirmation, lifting and positioning, and equipment checks and records to procedure, producing reviewable operation and inspection records); keep safety and authorization boundaries under control (personnel isolation, load and rigging limits, stopping and escalating on abnormalities, and not overstepping to approve lifting plans or modify equipment); and carry definable position responsibility (be responsible for your own operations and records, while referring matters beyond operating authorization to qualified personnel or supervisors under institutional rules). It is recommended to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a step-by-step work plan and inspection record, or one drill on recognizing and handling common abnormalities), rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

The daily work of hoist and winch operators can be broken down along three lines: (1) pre-job preparation—receiving the task, verifying the load and rigging, checking the equipment and brakes, and confirming signals and personnel positions; (2) operation—operating the drum to wind and unwind cable per signals, lifting and pulling, positioning and unloading; (3) inspection and maintenance—using hand tools to repair and adjust equipment, maintaining inspection records, and wrapping up and handing over after the job. The three lines share the same set of safety and inspection requirements, but their deliverables go to different recipients: preparation and operation serve the site work, while inspection and maintenance serve equipment and safety records.

Core task importance (O*NET): signaling and assisting with loading and unloading 83, verifying load position or depth 83, winding and unwinding cable 82, brake locking 82, and using hand tools to repair, maintain, and adjust equipment 82. entries: Load and signals | Load verification and signal confirmation | Select loads by weight and size specifications, and observe equipment gauges and indicators and others' hand signals to verify load position or depth (O*NET importance: signaling and assisting with loading and unloading materials 83, verifying load position or depth 83, selecting loads by specifications 79).

Drum operation | Lifting, pulling, and speed regulation | Start the crane or winch engine, use levers and pedals to wind or unwind cable on the drum, and adjust drum speed in response to hand signals, bells, buzzers, telephones, horns, or whistles (O*NET importance: operating levers and pedals to wind and unwind cable 82, responding to signals to adjust speed 80).
Braking and locking | Braking and locking loads | Use hand or foot brakes and move levers to lock the crane or winch (O*NET importance: using hand or foot brakes and locking 82).

Rigging and auxiliary equipment | Rigging connections and auxiliary work | Operate auxiliary equipment such as jacks, slings, cables, and chocks, and use hand tools to connect, secure, and disconnect cables or ropes from loads, materials, and equipment (O*NET importance: operating auxiliary equipment 81, connecting, securing, and disconnecting cables 73).

Equipment maintenance | Inspection, repair, and adjustment | Use hand tools to repair, maintain, and adjust equipment, and inspect equipment, structures, and materials before work to identify problems (O*NET importance: using hand tools to repair, maintain, and adjust 82, inspecting equipment and structures 74).

Equipment operation and setup | Multi-power and vehicle-mounted equipment | Operate compressed-air, diesel, electric, gasoline, or steam-driven cranes or winches, and climb ladders to set up vehicle-mounted cranes, or move and reposition cranes, winches, and loads (O*NET importance: operating multiple power-driven devices 84, climbing ladders to set up vehicle-mounted cranes 74, moving or repositioning equipment 74).

subject.name: Hoist and Winch Operators
subject.summary: Hoist and Winch Operators corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 53-7041.00 occupation "Hoist and Winch Operators": operating or tending hoists or winches to lift and pull loads using power-operated cable equipment. Official scope text: Operate or tend hoists or winches to lift and pull loads using power-operated cable equipment. Core tasks include signaling and assisting with loading and unloading materials (importance 83), observing equipment gauges and others' hand signals to verify load position or depth (83), using levers and pedals to wind or unwind cable on the drum (82), and using hand or foot brakes and locking (82). The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET (the precise occupation 53-7041.00); the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; China's work safety and special equipment institutional boundaries are labeled separately.
